title: Upload, transcode, deliver — and why bytes skip your API
description: The application tier issues a credential and records metadata. The file itself goes straight to object storage, and the expensive transcoding happens asynchronously afterwards.

steps.text: The client asks the API for permission. The API authorises, records metadata, and returns a pre-signed URL — a time-limited credential to write one object.

The file goes straight to object storage in chunks, never touching the application tier — routing gigabytes through your API wastes bandwidth and occupies connections for minutes. Chunking pays three ways: a failed part retries alone, parts upload in parallel, and an interrupted upload resumes. Naming each chunk by its content hash makes the upload verifiable and deduplicates identical chunks for free.
Transcoding is enqueued, not done inline. The uploader's request has already returned.

One job per rendition — 240p through 4K — plus side jobs for thumbnails and captions. They are independent and embarrassingly parallel, which is why spot instances suit them: an evicted job simply retries.

Each rendition is written back as segments of a few seconds, and a manifest lists what exists. Because most uploads are barely watched, generating the full ladder eagerly wastes most of the spend — produce a couple of common renditions now and the rest on first demand.
The first viewer in a region misses at the edge and the CDN pulls segments from origin.

Everyone after them is served from the edge. The player reads the manifest, starts conservatively, measures its own throughput, and switches rendition between segments — so quality changes rather than stalling when the network does.
